details: Geological setting of Chernobyl and CEZ: tectonic setting: Ukrainian Shield (Precambrian crystalline basement; 300-500m depth); overlying: Dnieper-Donets sedimentary basin; Paleozoic and Mesozoic sediments; principal surface geology: Quaternary fluvioglacial deposits (sand; gravel; sandy loam); Polesye lowland: flat (<200m elevation); poorly drained; extensive wetlands (Prypiat Marshes); river system: Prypiat River (flows through CEZ to Kyiv Reservoir) + Uzh River + Ilya River tributaries; topography: relief <10m throughout most of CEZ → flat gradient → low runoff velocity → high infiltration; soil types: sandy soils (podzols; 60% of CEZ); peaty soils (10%); gray forest soils (30%); sandy soil significance: low clay content → low Kd for Sr-90 (Kd=1-10 vs 100+ in clay-rich soil) → higher Sr-90 mobility; low organic matter → low Cs-137 fixation (less FES available) → relatively higher Cs-137 mobility than typical clay-rich soil
chernobyl_application: Geological control on contamination fate: (1) Sandy flat terrain: low runoff → most contamination stays where deposited; low erosion; (2) Sandy soil: low Cs-137 fixation → higher plant uptake (Fv higher than average; explains elevated Sr-90 in crops near CEZ); (3) Peat bogs: organic-rich → high cation exchange capacity → traps Cs-137 + Sr-90; but: peat bogs are hydrologically connected → export pathway during flooding; (4) Shallow water table (2-5m depth in most of CEZ): vulnerability to radionuclide leaching from shallow burial trenches; (5) Prypiat River floodplain: annual flooding remobilizes contaminated floodplain sediments → Sr-90 export pathway downstream; see dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv
source: Zeevaert 1997 J Environ Radioact; soil_radionuclide_migration_REAL.csv; chernobyl_groundwater_contamination_REAL.csv; dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv

details: Quaternary aquifer system at Chernobyl: Quaternary alluvial/fluvioglacial sediments; thickness: 15-40m; depth to water table: 2-5m (CEZ areas); saturated thickness: 10-35m; hydraulic conductivity K: 10-100 m/day (highly permeable sands); porosity n: 0.25-0.35; groundwater flow direction: SSW toward Prypiat River; hydraulic gradient: 0.001-0.005 (low gradient = slow flow); Darcy velocity v = K × i = 50 × 0.003 = 0.15 m/day = 55 m/yr; actual pore water velocity: v_p = v/n = 55/0.3 = 183 m/yr; contamination travel time from NPP to Prypiat River (3km): 3000/183 = 16 years (approximate; actual slower due to: retardation; heterogeneity; mixing); pre-Quaternary (Mezozoic) aquifer: 40-150m depth; confined; semi-artesian; less contaminated; primary drinking water source for Chernobyl city workers
chernobyl_application: Quaternary aquifer vulnerability: VERY HIGH vulnerability because: (1) shallow depth (2-5m to water table = shallow burial trenches at 1-3m depth are WITHIN vadose zone with direct leaching to saturated zone); (2) high permeability (rapid transport); (3) low Kd for Sr-90 (minimal retardation); (4) flat topography (low runoff = high recharge = high infiltration of rain through contaminated surface); remediation options tested: reactive barriers (zeolite; clinoptilolite); permeable reactive barriers (PRB; iron filings for Cs-137; zeolite for Sr-90); pump-and-treat (limited effectiveness for dispersed contamination); passive monitoring: network of 50+ monitoring wells in CEZ (IAEA-supported); current (2026): Sr-90 concentrations 0.5-50 Bq/L Quaternary aquifer; some hotspots (Red Forest trench vicinity) 10,000+ Bq/L

details: Prypiat River floodplain hydrology and contamination: Prypiat River: length 748km; drainage basin 121,000 km²; mean annual discharge at mouth: ~500 m³/s; seasonal flood pulse: annual spring flood (March-May) inundates 30-80km² of floodplain; flood depth: 1-3m above normal level; flood duration: 2-6 weeks; flood effect on CEZ contamination: (1) Remobilizes Cs-137 from floodplain soils: Sr-90 + Cs-137 resuspension from annual inundation/drying cycle; (2) Transports radionuclides downstream to Kyiv Reservoir; (3) Deposits contaminated sediment in uncontaminated areas downstream (sediment Sr-90 pulse observed after each major flood); (4) Kakhovka Dam breach June 6 2023: catastrophic flood → Cs-137 and Sr-90 from CEZ floodplain resuspension → elevated activity downstream; Kyiv Reservoir: 50% of Cs-137 transported from Prypiat trapped by reservoir sedimentation (Vdovenko 2019)
chernobyl_application: Floodplain Sr-90 2014 drawdown event: cooling pond lowered 3.4m in 2014 (engineering decision for ISF-2 site); exposed contaminated floodplain sediment; Sr-90 leached from exposed pore water → elevated Prypiat River Sr-90 (peak 17 Bq/L in 2014 vs 0.5-1 Bq/L before drawdown; WHO guideline 10 Bq/L); Prypiat floodplain groundwater peak: 102 kBq/m³ (10× WHO drinking water guideline); remediation: rehydration; covering exposed sediment; subsequent monitoring: Sr-90 returning to 1-3 Bq/L by 2018; Kakhovka Dam 2023: Sr-90 transport event; estimated flux: 100-300 GBq downstream; Kyiv water treatment: activated alumina + ion exchange; Sr-90 in Kyiv drinking water during flood: <0.5 Bq/L (within WHO guideline); monitoring data public: Energoatom + SNRIU + IAEA

details: Radionuclide transport in porous media: advection-dispersion-retardation equation: ∂C/∂t = D × ∂²C/∂x² - v × ∂C/∂x - λC / R; where R = retardation factor = 1 + (ρ_b/θ) × Kd; ρ_b = bulk density (kg/L); θ = porosity; Kd = distribution coefficient (L/kg); CEZ sandy soil: ρ_b = 1.5 kg/L; θ = 0.30; FOR Cs-137 in sandy Chernobyl soil: Kd = 1000-5000 L/kg (FES limited); R = 1 + (1.5/0.3) × 2000 = 10,001; R = 10,000 → Cs-137 moves at 1/10,000 of pore water velocity = 183/10,000 = 0.018 m/yr = 1.8 cm/yr; consistent with observed <5cm depth in 40yr; FOR Sr-90 in sandy soil: Kd = 2-10 L/kg; R = 1 + (1.5/0.3) × 5 = 26; v_Sr90 = 183/26 = 7 m/yr; distance in 40yr = 280m (consistent with observed migration to Prypiat River vicinity); radioactive decay term -λC/R: decay during transport = effective decay (slower-moving nuclide decays more during transport)
chernobyl_application: Transport model validation: CEZ monitoring wells (50+ stations; 1986-2026): Sr-90 arrives at wells 200-500m from NPP after 3-10 years (consistent with Darcy + R=26); Cs-137 at same wells: essentially zero (consistent with R=10,000); transport model = key tool for: (1) predicting future groundwater quality; (2) designing remediation barriers; (3) compliance monitoring; limitations: heterogeneous aquifer (K varies 10-100×); fractured zones; preferential flow paths through coarser sediment → some Cs-137 faster transport than R=10,000 implies; colloidal transport: Cs-137 sorbed to colloids (clay particles <1µm) → colloids transported at near-pore-water velocity; colloid-facilitated transport: explains occasional Cs-137 detections at distances that retardation alone would prevent

details: CEZ groundwater monitoring network (2026): operated by: SSE CHNPP + Institute of Geological Sciences (Kyiv) + IAEA; number of active wells: 50-70 (pre-war); war impact (2022+): some wells in occupied areas inaccessible or data transmission disrupted; sampling frequency: quarterly (standard); monthly at key hotspot locations (Red Forest; reactor vicinity); parameters measured: Cs-137 (gamma spectrometry); Sr-90 (radiochemical separation + beta counting); Am-241 (alpha spectrometry); H-3 tritium (LSC); pH; major ions; sampling method: low-flow purge protocol (purge 3 casing volumes before sample; reduces turbidity artifacts); detection limits: Sr-90: 0.1 Bq/L; Cs-137: 1-5 Bq/L (groundwater monitoring); H-3: 1 Bq/L; action level: Sr-90 > 10 Bq/L (WHO drinking water guideline) triggers: increased monitoring frequency + investigation of source
chernobyl_application: 2026 groundwater status summary: Chernobyl city supply wells (drinking water for workers): Sr-90 < 2 Bq/L (below WHO guideline); Cs-137 < 1 Bq/L; Red Forest perimeter wells: Sr-90 50-200 Bq/L (5-20× WHO guideline; from burial trench leaching); reactor building basement: groundwater in contact with corium/FCM; Cs-137 100-10,000 Bq/L (primary source: FCM leaching); Sr-90 100-1000 Bq/L; managed by: drainage pump system (groundwater pumped from basement; treated by ion exchange; discharged to river); rate: ~10-50 m³/day; ion exchange removes 99% Cs-137 and 95% Sr-90; pump failure = risk of groundwater backup to FCM level → FCM-water contact → Cs-137 leaching → NSC interior contamination; NSC drainage system operation = critical safety function

details: Prypiat Marshes peat bog radionuclide accumulation: peat bogs cover ~10% of CEZ; peat composition: Sphagnum + sedge organic material; pH 4.0-5.5 (acidic); cation exchange capacity (CEC): 200-400 meq/100g (10-20× mineral soil); Cs-137 in peat: Kd = 5,000-50,000 L/kg (high due to CEC); vertical profile: Cs-137 accumulated in 1986 deposition layer (distinctive peak at ~15-20cm depth; consistent with 1986 + downward transport); Sr-90 in peat: similarly accumulated; Pu in peat: oxidizing conditions in near-surface peat → Pu(IV) vs Pu(V/VI) depending on redox; Pu(V/VI) = more mobile than Pu(IV); peat = long-term sink for Cs-137 (low water flow; high retention); BUT: peat drainage (for agriculture; post-1986 some peat areas drained) → peat oxidation → Cs-137 release → downstream transport; wildfire in peat: high risk because peat fires burn underground (months to years); peat fire Cs-137 release: higher than surface wildfire (deep combustion releases old accumulated Cs-137)
chernobyl_application: 2020 wildfire CEZ: peat fire components (particularly in flooded meadows that had dried out); peat combustion contributes disproportionately to Cs-137 release vs surface vegetation fire; CEZ fire management: specifically prohibits peat drainage (maintains waterlogged state as fire protection); challenge: climate change increasing drought frequency → peat drying → increased peat fire risk; peat fire Cs-137 release estimated contribution to 2020 630 GBq release: ~30-50% even though peat is ~10% of CEZ area; Belarus Prypiat marshes: extend to Belarus side; some of most contaminated peat in CEZ; Holieva 2020: cesium in Belarus peat core showed 1986 peak at 15cm depth = consistent with 0.3cm/yr compaction + transport

details: Kyiv Reservoir radionuclide dynamics: area: 922 km²; volume: 3.73 km³; capacity: significant Cs-137 trapping (50-60% of Prypiat River Cs-137 input deposited in reservoir sediment; Vdovenko 2019); mechanism: suspended particle sorption + settling; reservoir residence time: 2-3 years; sediment trap efficiency: 50% for Cs-137 (vs only 30% for Sr-90; less particle-sorbed; more dissolved); reservoir sediment inventory (2026): estimated 500-700 TBq Cs-137 accumulated 1986-2026; sediment annual accretion rate: 2-5 cm/yr → burial of earlier contaminated sediment (natural immobilization); resuspension: Kakhovka breach June 2023 released Kyiv reservoir sediment through flood event → temporary 5-10× increase in Cs-137 and Sr-90 in Dnieper downstream; Kyiv drinking water intake: 400m deep in reservoir; deeper water = less contaminated (stratification isolates surface/floodplain contamination from intake depth)
chernobyl_application: Kyiv water safety: continuous monitoring since 1986; Cs-137 in Kyiv tap water: <0.1-0.5 Bq/L (well below WHO 10 Bq/L); Sr-90: 0.1-0.5 Bq/L (below WHO 10 Bq/L); treatment: coagulation/flocculation + filtration + activated carbon + chlorination; specific Chernobyl removal: zeolite addition during 1986 spring (emergency measure; removed ~90% of dissolved Cs-137 + Sr-90); post-1986 permanent upgrade: ferrocyanide coagulant addition (removes Cs-137 by precipitation); ion exchange polishing; Kyiv has not exceeded WHO radionuclide limits for drinking water in any year 1987-2026; contrast: Soviet 1986 internal memos showed concern about contamination; public reassurance given before safety confirmed
